name: Oil
plain: Olive oil was food, medicine, lamp fuel and cosmetic in Israel. Because it was poured on kings, priests and sacred objects to set them apart for God, it became a picture of being chosen and equipped by God, and of joy and healing.

meanings.meaning: Consecration: set apart for God's service
meanings.note: A special holy anointing oil was mixed for the tabernacle and priests and was forbidden for ordinary use. Pouring oil on a person marked them as God's chosen servant.

meanings.meaning: Association with the Spirit of God
meanings.note: When Samuel anointed David, the Spirit came on him from that day. Isaiah links being anointed with having the Spirit, and Jesus applies this to himself. The Bible links oil and Spirit closely but never states a formula that oil equals the Spirit.
Oil on the head was a sign of festivity and welcome; the 'oil of joy' replaces mourning.
Oil was ordinary first-aid. In James, elders anoint the sick with prayer; whether the oil is medicinal, symbolic or sacramental is debated between traditions.

otUsage: Oil appears in daily life (bread, lamps, skin) and in worship: grain offerings were mixed with it, the lampstand burned it, and kings, priests and the tabernacle were anointed with it. A full supply of oil is a sign of covenant blessing (Deut 7:13), and its loss a sign of judgement.
ntUsage: The title Christ (Greek christos) means 'anointed one'. Jesus is said to be anointed with the Spirit rather than with literal oil, and believers share an 'anointing' from God (2 Cor 1:21; 1 John 2:20). The disciples and later the elders used oil with prayer for the sick.
caution: In the parable of the ten virgins (Matt 25:1-13) the oil is often read as the Holy Spirit, good works or genuine faith; the parable itself does not say, so hold any single reading loosely. Modern talk of 'the anointing' as a transferable power goes beyond what these texts state.

name: Bread
plain: Bread was the basic food of the ancient world, so it stands for life itself and for God's daily provision. Jesus took this ordinary food and called himself 'the bread of life', and gave bread to his followers as a sign of his body.

meanings.note: Manna in the wilderness taught Israel to depend on God one day at a time; the Lord's Prayer asks for 'daily bread'.
People do not live by bread alone but by every word from God; a 'famine of hearing the word' is worse than a food famine.

meanings.meaning: Jesus as the bread of life
meanings.note: Jesus contrasts himself with the manna: whoever comes to him will not hunger. How far John 6 refers to the Lord's Supper is debated.
Twelve loaves (the 'bread of the Presence') lay before God in the holy place. At the Last Supper bread signifies Christ's body, and 'one loaf' expresses the unity of the church.
At Passover Israel ate bread without yeast because they left Egypt in a hurry; Paul applies this to removing 'old leaven' of malice from the church.

otUsage: Bread is hospitality (Gen 18:5-6), wages, sacrifice and provision. Manna, the bread of the Presence and the feast of Unleavened Bread give bread a central place in Israel's worship and memory.
ntUsage: Jesus feeds crowds with a few loaves, teaches his disciples to ask for daily bread, calls himself the bread of life, and institutes the Lord's Supper with bread. The early church 'broke bread' together.
caution: What exactly the bread of the Lord's Supper is (Christ's body really present, a spiritual presence, or a memorial sign) is one of the major debates of church history; see /debates/lords-supper.

name: Wine
original: Hebrew yayin, tirosh (new wine); Greek oinos
plain: Wine in the Bible is a gift that gladdens people and a sign of God's abundant blessing, especially at feasts. It is also a warning image: drunkenness ruins people, and God's judgement is pictured as a cup of wine that makes nations stagger.

meanings.note: Plentiful grain, wine and oil is the standard picture of a blessed land.
The prophets picture the coming age as a feast with the finest wine; Jesus' first sign is turning water into a huge quantity of good wine at a wedding.
At the Last Supper the cup of wine signifies Christ's blood poured out for forgiveness.
Judgement is a strong wine that makes the nations stagger, or a winepress in which grapes are trodden.
Drunkenness is consistently condemned; Paul contrasts being drunk with wine and being filled with the Spirit.

otUsage: Wine is part of offerings (Num 15:5), feasts and ordinary meals. Nazirites and priests on duty abstained (Num 6:3; Lev 10:9). Israel is pictured as God's vineyard, and its failure as sour grapes (Isa 5:1-7).
ntUsage: Jesus drinks wine and is accused of being a drunkard by his critics (Matt 11:19). New wine needs new wineskins (Mark 2:22), a picture of the newness of the kingdom. The cup of the Lord's Supper holds wine.
caution: Biblical wine was fermented and could make people drunk. Some Christians argue that 'new wine' or diluted wine differs from modern alcohol and favour abstinence; others hold moderate drinking is permitted. The texts condemn drunkenness clearly; total abstinence is a debated application.

name: Cup
plain: A cup is what someone is given to drink, so it came to mean the experience or destiny God hands to a person: blessing for some, judgement for others. Jesus called his coming suffering 'the cup'.

meanings.note: The LORD is David's 'cup'; his cup overflows with good things.
Nations who oppose God must drink a cup that makes them stagger.
In Gethsemane Jesus prays for the cup to pass but accepts it. Many read this as Jesus taking the cup of wrath meant for others; others stress suffering and martyrdom more broadly.
The cup of the Lord's Supper is a 'cup of blessing' and the new covenant in Christ's blood.

otUsage: Cups appear at meals and in the Passover-like thanksgiving of the Psalms, and as a common prophetic image for judgement on Judah and the nations.
ntUsage: Jesus takes the cup at the Last Supper, prays about 'this cup' in Gethsemane, and asks James and John if they can drink his cup. Revelation pictures Babylon holding a golden cup of abominations (Rev 17:4) and receiving God's cup of wrath.
caution: The Passover meal in later Jewish practice has four cups; linking specific Gospel cups to these (for example Luke 22:17 and 22:20) is a common suggestion, but the rabbinic order is documented later than the New Testament, so treat it as possible rather than certain.

name: Salt
plain: Salt preserved food, gave it flavour and was part of making agreements by sharing a meal. So it stands for lasting covenant loyalty and for the good influence God's people should have. Salted land, on the other hand, was barren, so salt can also mean judgement.

meanings.note: Offerings were to be salted with 'the salt of the covenant'; a 'covenant of salt' means one that is permanent.
Jesus calls his followers the salt of the earth and warns against losing saltiness. Whether he means preservation, flavour, or both is debated; the text does not specify.
Speech 'seasoned with salt' is attractive and thoughtful.
Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt; a land 'sown with salt' is ruined.
Elisha heals Jericho's water with salt; newborns were rubbed with salt.

otUsage: Salt is required in offerings, describes unbreakable covenants, and marks both healing (Elisha) and devastation (Sodom, Abimelech's Shechem). The Dead Sea is called the Salt Sea (Gen 14:3).
ntUsage: Jesus' 'salt of the earth' saying, his puzzling 'everyone will be salted with fire' (Mark 9:49), and Paul's advice on speech.
caution: Ancient salt from the Dead Sea area was often mixed with other minerals and could lose its taste as the salt leached out; that explains Jesus' image better than modern pure table salt.

name: Lamp and lampstand
original: Hebrew ner (lamp), menorah (lampstand); Greek luchnos, luchnia
plain: In a world without electric light, a lamp meant safety, life and the ability to see the way. The seven-branched golden lampstand in the tabernacle stood for God's light among his people, and later the churches are pictured as lampstands giving light to the world.

meanings.meaning: God's light and presence in the sanctuary
meanings.note: The lampstand burned continually before the LORD; its almond-blossom design may echo a flowering tree.
Scripture is a lamp for one's feet: enough light for the next step.
God promises David 'a lamp' in Jerusalem, meaning his dynasty will not be snuffed out.
Zechariah's lampstand is fed by the Spirit; in Revelation the seven lampstands are explicitly the seven churches, and the two witnesses are two lampstands.
Keeping lamps burning means being ready for the Master's return.

otUsage: The menorah in the tabernacle and Solomon's ten lampstands (1 Kgs 7:49) mark God's dwelling. The lamp is also a picture of human life ('the lamp of the wicked will be put out', Prov 24:20) and of David's dynasty.
ntUsage: Jesus warns not to hide a lamp under a basket (Mark 4:21), calls John the Baptist 'a burning and shining lamp' (John 5:35), and threatens to remove the Ephesian church's lampstand if it does not repent (Rev 2:5). In the new Jerusalem the Lamb is its lamp (Rev 21:23).
caution: The Hanukkah lampstand (nine branches) is a later Jewish development; the biblical menorah has seven lamps.

name: Key(s)
plain: Whoever holds the keys controls who gets in and who stays out. In the Bible keys picture authority: to open and shut the king's house, the kingdom of heaven, or even death itself.

meanings.meaning: Delegated authority in the king's house
meanings.note: Eliakim, the palace steward, receives the key of David's house; Revelation applies this key to the risen Christ.

meanings.meaning: Keys of the kingdom given to Peter
meanings.note: Catholics read this as a unique, continuing office passed to Peter's successors, the popes. Orthodox usually see Peter as first among equals and the keys shared by all bishops. Protestants commonly link the keys to preaching the gospel and church discipline exercised by the whole church (Matt 18:18 gives binding and loosing to the disciples generally).
Jesus accuses the lawyers of taking away the key of knowledge: neither entering nor letting others in.
Jesus holds the keys of death and Hades; an angel receives the key of the bottomless pit.

otUsage: Keys are rare in the Old Testament; the key passage is Isaiah 22, where palace authority passes from Shebna to Eliakim.
ntUsage: Matthew 16 (Peter), Luke 11 (key of knowledge) and Revelation's keys of David, death and the abyss.
caution: Matthew 16:19 is a classic flashpoint between Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant views of church authority; read each position at its best. See /debates/scripture-and-tradition.

name: Crown
original: Hebrew atarah, nezer; Greek stephanos (victor's wreath), diadema (royal diadem)
plain: A crown marks a king, a priest set apart, or a winner at the games. In the Bible it stands for royal rule, honour, and the reward God gives to the faithful; it also appears mocking Jesus as a crown of thorns.

meanings.note: Christ returns wearing 'many diadems', the Greek word for royal crowns.
The high priest's turban bore a gold plate called the 'holy crown'. Zechariah crowns the high priest Joshua in a sign of a coming priest-king.
Humanity is crowned with glory; a good wife, grey hair and grandchildren are crowns.
Paul uses the athlete's victory wreath. Whether these 'crowns' are distinct rewards or different ways of describing eternal life itself is debated.
Soldiers crown Jesus with thorns; John's Gospel presents the mock coronation as ironically true.

otUsage: Crowns belong to kings and to the high priest, and are used figuratively for honour. Losing one's crown means disgrace (Lam 5:16).
ntUsage: Mostly stephanos, the victor's wreath, for believers' reward, and the crown of thorns. The elders cast their crowns before God's throne (Rev 4:10), giving their honour back to him.

name: Sword
plain: The sword is the main weapon of ancient war, so it means violence, judgement and the power of rulers. The Bible also uses it for God's word, which cuts deep and judges truly.

meanings.note: Sword, famine and plague are the standard triad of covenant curses.
The Spirit's sword is the word of God; the returning Christ conquers with a sword from his mouth, not one in his hand.

meanings.meaning: Authority of the state to punish
meanings.note: The ruler 'does not bear the sword in vain'. How far this justifies war or capital punishment divides Christian traditions, especially pacifist and just-war ones.
Jesus says he brings 'not peace but a sword', meaning his call will divide families. Simeon tells Mary a sword will pierce her soul.
A flaming sword guards the way to the tree of life.

otUsage: Swords fill Israel's battle narratives. The prophets look forward to swords beaten into ploughshares (Isa 2:4; Mic 4:3), though Joel reverses the image for the final battle (Joel 3:10).
ntUsage: Peter's sword in Gethsemane is rebuked: 'all who take the sword will perish by the sword' (Matt 26:52). The 'two swords' of Luke 22:38 are debated: literal self-defence, or a sign that the disciples misunderstood. Paul's armour image includes the sword of the Spirit.
caution: Medieval 'two swords' theory (spiritual and temporal power) built a whole political theology on Luke 22:38; most interpreters today think that goes far beyond the verse.

name: Trumpet / shofar
original: Hebrew shofar (ram's horn), chatsotsrah (metal trumpet); Greek salpinx
plain: A trumpet blast gathered people, warned of danger, started battles, crowned kings and announced holy days. In the Bible it signals that God is acting: at Sinai, at Jericho, and at the end of the age when the dead are raised.

meanings.note: Silver trumpets assembled the camp; the watchman blows the trumpet to warn of attack.
At Sinai a very loud trumpet sound grew louder as God descended.
The ram's horn announced the year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and land returned.
Jericho's walls fall at the trumpet; kings were proclaimed with it.

meanings.meaning: The end of the age and resurrection
meanings.note: The 'last trumpet' raises the dead. Revelation's seven trumpets announce escalating judgements.

otUsage: Ram's horn and silver trumpets mark worship, war, coronation and the Day of Trumpets. The prophets use the trumpet for the coming day of the LORD.
ntUsage: Trumpets accompany Christ's return, the resurrection, and the seven judgements of Revelation 8 to 11.
caution: Whether Paul's 'last trumpet' is the same as Revelation's seventh trumpet, and how either fits a timeline of rapture and tribulation, is debated; see /debates/rapture.

name: Seal
plain: A seal was a carved stone or ring pressed into clay or wax. It proved who owned or authorised something and kept it closed. The Bible uses it for ownership, protection, authenticity and secrets kept until the right time.

meanings.note: Letters and deeds were valid when sealed with the owner's seal.
God's servants are marked on the forehead and spared from judgement.

meanings.meaning: The Holy Spirit as God's seal
meanings.note: The Spirit marks believers as God's and guarantees their future. Whether this sealing implies the believer can never fall away is part of the /debates/eternal-security discussion.
Daniel is told to seal his book; in Revelation only the Lamb can open the sealed scroll, and John is told not to seal his.
Circumcision was a seal of the righteousness Abraham had by faith. Some traditions apply this to baptism.

otUsage: Royal and personal seals appear in Genesis (Judah's signet, Gen 38:18), Kings, Esther and Jeremiah. Daniel's den was sealed (Dan 6:17); the beloved asks to be set 'as a seal upon your heart' (Song 8:6).
ntUsage: Jesus' tomb is sealed (Matt 27:66); the Father has 'set his seal' on the Son (John 6:27); the Spirit seals believers; Revelation has seven seals opened by the Lamb.

name: Horn
plain: An animal's horn is its weapon and the sign of its strength. In the Bible a horn can be a literal container for oil, the corners of the altar, or a picture of power, especially royal power. In Daniel and Revelation horns are kings.

meanings.note: To 'lift up the horn' is to be strengthened or vindicated; God is the 'horn of my salvation'.
Zechariah praises God for raising 'a horn of salvation' in David's house.
Daniel's angel explains that horns are kings. The Lamb with seven horns (Rev 5:6) has complete power.
Samuel and Zadok anoint kings from a horn of oil.

meanings.meaning: Horns of the altar: atonement and refuge
meanings.note: Blood was put on the altar's horns; a fugitive grasping them sought mercy, though the law did not protect deliberate murderers (Exod 21:14).

otUsage: Horn imagery runs from Hannah's song and the Psalms (strength) to the altar's corner horns and the ram caught by its horns in place of Isaac (Gen 22:13).
ntUsage: Only Luke 1:69 outside Revelation; in Revelation the Lamb, the dragon and the beasts all have horns, showing a contest of powers.
caution: Identifying the 'little horn' of Daniel 7 and 8 is debated: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (most critical and many conservative scholars for Dan 8), a future antichrist, or the papacy (a historic Protestant reading). See /debates/millennium.

name: Scroll / book
original: Hebrew sefer, megillah; Greek biblion, biblos
plain: Ancient books were rolled scrolls of leather or papyrus. In the Bible a scroll stands for God's recorded word, his plan for history, and his record of people and their deeds, including the 'book of life'.

meanings.note: God's register of those who belong to him. Whether names can be blotted out is part of the /debates/eternal-security discussion.
Books are opened at the judgement; God remembers those who fear him.
Only the Lamb is worthy to open the sealed scroll, so only Christ unlocks and carries out God's purposes.
Prophets eat a scroll: sweet in the mouth but sometimes bitter in the stomach, because the message includes judgement.
The sky is rolled up like a scroll at the end.

otUsage: Moses writes the law in a book (Exod 24:7; Deut 31:24-26); Josiah's reform starts when the book of the law is found (2 Kgs 22:8-13); King Jehoiakim cuts and burns Jeremiah's scroll, which is rewritten (Jer 36).
ntUsage: Jesus reads from the Isaiah scroll in Nazareth (Luke 4:17-21). Revelation's sealed scroll, little scroll and books of judgement form a major thread. Paul asks Timothy for his scrolls and parchments (2 Tim 4:13).

name: Rod / staff
original: Hebrew matteh, shevet, maqqel; Greek rhabdos
plain: A shepherd's staff, a walking stick, a ruler's sceptre and a rod for correction were all similar wooden sticks. So the rod stands for authority, guidance and protection, and sometimes for discipline or punishment.

meanings.meaning: God's power working through a leader
meanings.note: Moses' ordinary shepherd's staff becomes 'the staff of God' through which signs are done.
The sceptre will not depart from Judah; the Messiah rules the nations with a rod of iron.
The rod drove off predators and the staff guided the sheep; both comfort.
Aaron's staff buds, blossoms and bears almonds, settling who is the true priest; it was kept in the ark.
Fathers and God himself discipline with the rod; Assyria is the rod of God's anger.

otUsage: Staffs of Moses and Aaron, the sceptre of Judah, the shepherd's rod and the rod of correction all appear. Isaiah's 'rod out of the stem of Jesse' (Isa 11:1, KJV) is a different word meaning a shoot.
ntUsage: Jesus sends the disciples out with only a staff (Mark 6:8). Revelation applies Psalm 2's iron rod to Christ and his faithful people, and John measures the temple with a measuring rod (Rev 11:1).
caution: Whether the Proverbs 'rod' passages endorse physical punishment of children today is debated: some read them as permanent instruction, others as ancient wisdom about discipline in general that need not mean hitting.

name: Yoke
plain: A yoke is the wooden beam that joins two oxen so they can pull a plough together. It became a picture of being under someone's control, whether a cruel master or a kind teacher, and of working in partnership.

meanings.note: God broke Israel's yoke in Egypt; Jeremiah wore a yoke to act out submission to Babylon.

meanings.meaning: Obligation to God and his law
meanings.note: Jewish teachers spoke of taking on 'the yoke of the kingdom of heaven' (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). At the Jerusalem council Peter calls law-keeping as a requirement for Gentiles a yoke too heavy to bear.
Jesus invites the weary to take his yoke: becoming his disciple brings rest, not a heavier load.
Do not be 'unequally yoked'; Paul calls a coworker his 'true yokefellow'.

otUsage: Mostly a picture of foreign domination and of God's freeing his people. Isaiah 58:6 calls true fasting breaking every yoke.
ntUsage: Jesus' gentle yoke, Paul's warning against a 'yoke of slavery', and the image of believers as yoked partners.
caution: 2 Corinthians 6:14 is often applied to marriage between a believer and unbeliever; the context is broader (partnership with idolatry), though many still apply it to marriage.

name: Altar
original: Hebrew mizbeach ('place of slaughter'); Greek thusiasterion
plain: An altar is a raised place where offerings were made to God. It marked meeting with God, remembering what he had done, and atonement for sin through sacrifice.

meanings.note: The patriarchs built altars where God appeared to them.
Blood on the altar made atonement because 'the life is in the blood'.
An altar could be a witness rather than a place of sacrifice; altars were named 'The LORD is my banner' and 'The LORD is peace'.
In Revelation the martyrs cry out under the altar and the prayers of the saints rise from it.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians often connect this with the Eucharistic table; many Protestants read it as Christ and his cross, since Hebrews stresses that Christ's sacrifice was once for all. Debated.

otUsage: From Noah and Abraham to the bronze altar of the tabernacle and temple, altars structure Israel's worship. Unauthorised altars and pagan altars are condemned (1 Kgs 12:32-33; 2 Kgs 23:15).
ntUsage: Jesus tells worshippers to reconcile before offering at the altar (Matt 5:23-24). Hebrews presents Christ's single sacrifice as replacing repeated offerings; Paul urges believers to offer themselves as 'living sacrifices' (Rom 12:1).

name: Incense
original: Hebrew qetoret, levonah (frankincense); Greek thumiama, libanos
plain: Incense is fragrant resin burned to produce sweet smoke. In the tabernacle it was offered morning and evening before God, and the Bible links its rising smoke to prayer rising to God.

meanings.note: The people prayed outside while Zechariah offered incense; in Revelation the golden bowls of incense are the prayers of the saints.
The holy incense had a set recipe and was not for private use. Nadab and Abihu died offering 'strange fire'.
On the Day of Atonement incense clouded the mercy seat; Aaron's censer stopped a plague as he stood between the living and the dead.
Christ's self-giving and the apostles' lives are a fragrance to God; Malachi foresees incense offered to God among the nations.

otUsage: A golden incense altar stood before the veil. Incense offered to other gods, or by the wrong person, brought judgement (2 Chr 26:16-21; Jer 44:17-23).
ntUsage: Frankincense is among the Magi's gifts (Matt 2:11). Revelation pictures heavenly worship with incense, joining prayers to God's action on earth.
caution: Whether incense should be used in Christian worship today is a matter of tradition: Orthodox, Catholic and some Anglican churches use it; most Protestant churches do not, reading Revelation's incense as purely symbolic.

name: Veil (temple curtain)
plain: A thick embroidered curtain separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelt, from the rest of the tabernacle and temple. Only the high priest went behind it, once a year. When Jesus died, the Gospels say the temple curtain tore from top to bottom.

meanings.meaning: Separation between a holy God and sinful people
meanings.note: Hebrews says the curtain showed that 'the way into the holiest' was not yet open.

meanings.meaning: Access to God opened through Christ
meanings.note: Hebrews links the curtain to Christ's flesh: through his death believers may draw near with confidence.
Some scholars read the tearing mainly as a sign that God was leaving or judging the temple, anticipating its destruction; others combine both readings.
A different object. Paul uses Moses' veil for a lack of understanding that is removed when one turns to the Lord.

otUsage: Woven with cherubim, the veil echoed the cherubim guarding Eden. Isaiah promises God will destroy 'the veil that is spread over all nations' (Isa 25:7).
ntUsage: All three Synoptic Gospels record the tearing (Matt 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45). Hebrews builds a theology of access on it.
caution: Which curtain tore (the inner veil or the outer one at the entrance) is debated; Hebrews' interpretation fits the inner veil.

name: Ark of the covenant
plain: The ark was a gold-covered wooden chest kept in the Most Holy Place. It held the stone tablets of the law and was topped by the 'mercy seat' with two cherubim. It was treated as God's throne or footstool on earth, the place where he met his people.

meanings.note: God is 'enthroned between the cherubim'; the ark is his footstool.
It held the tablets of the law; manna and Aaron's staff were kept with it.

Blood was sprinkled on the lid on the Day of Atonement. Paul calls Christ a hilasterion, the Greek word used for the mercy seat; whether he means 'mercy seat', 'propitiation' or 'place of atonement' is discussed.
The ark could not be treated as a lucky charm (1 Sam 4) or handled carelessly.

Catholic and Orthodox tradition sees parallels between Mary carrying Jesus and David bringing the ark (leaping, 'how can the ark/mother of my Lord come to me', three months). Many Protestant scholars see the parallel as possible but unproven.

otUsage: The ark leads Israel across the Jordan (Josh 3), is captured and returned by the Philistines, brought to Jerusalem by David, and placed in Solomon's temple. It disappears from history, likely when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC; Jeremiah says a time will come when it is no longer missed (Jer 3:16).
ntUsage: Hebrews describes its contents; Revelation sees 'the ark of his covenant' in God's heavenly temple (Rev 11:19).
caution: Noah's ark is a different Hebrew word (tevah) and a different object. Claims that the ark of the covenant survives today (for example in Ethiopia, held by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church at Aksum) are traditions that cannot be checked.

name: Stones (memorial stones, cornerstone, living stones)
plain: Stones last, so people set them up to remember what God had done. God wrote his law on stone. The Bible also calls the Messiah the cornerstone and calls believers 'living stones' built into God's house.

meanings.note: Jacob's pillar at Bethel, the twelve stones from the Jordan, and Samuel's Ebenezer ('stone of help').

meanings.meaning: Law written in stone, and hearts of stone
meanings.note: God promises to replace a stony heart with a heart of flesh; Paul contrasts tablets of stone with the Spirit writing on hearts.
The New Testament applies the rejected stone to Jesus, now the key stone of God's building.
The same stone is a foundation for some and a stumbling block for others.
The church is a spiritual house built from people joined to Christ.
A stone 'cut without hands' crushes the statue of empires and becomes a mountain filling the earth.

otUsage: Altars of uncut stone, memorial heaps, stone tablets, and the stone that destroys the empires in Daniel. Stoning was also a method of execution (Lev 24:14).
ntUsage: The cornerstone texts are among the most quoted Old Testament passages in the New. Jesus says the stones would cry out if his disciples were silent (Luke 19:40); the risen Christ gives a white stone with a new name (Rev 2:17).

name: Water
plain: In a dry land water means life, but floods and deep seas mean danger and death. The Bible uses water both ways: as cleansing and new life, and as the chaos God conquers.

meanings.meaning: Chaos and death that God controls
meanings.note: Creation begins with God ordering the waters; the flood undoes creation; drowning is a picture of distress.
Washing with water removed ritual impurity; God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people.
John explains that the 'living water' Jesus promised meant the Spirit.
Israel passed through the sea, Noah through the flood; the New Testament compares this to baptism.

otUsage: Water from the rock, wells of the patriarchs, the bronze basin for priests, and Ezekiel's river flowing from the temple to heal the Dead Sea.
ntUsage: Jesus is baptised, walks on water, turns water into wine, offers living water, and washes feet. The new creation has the river of the water of life.
caution: What 'born of water and the Spirit' (John 3:5) means is debated: baptism, natural birth, or the cleansing work of the Spirit described in Ezek 36:25-27. See /debates/baptism.

name: Fire
plain: Fire gives light and warmth but also burns and destroys. The Bible uses it for God's holy presence, his judgement, the purifying of his people, and the Holy Spirit.

meanings.note: The burning bush, the pillar of fire and the fire on Sinai; 'our God is a consuming fire'.
Fire from the LORD consumed the offering.
Sodom, Nadab and Abihu, and the final judgement.
Like metal in a furnace, people and their work are tested and refined.

meanings.meaning: The Holy Spirit and God's word
meanings.note: Tongues like fire at Pentecost; God's word burns in Jeremiah's bones.

otUsage: God appears in fire; the altar fire was never to go out (Lev 6:13); judgement falls as fire. Daniel's friends survive the furnace with a fourth figure (Dan 3:25).
ntUsage: John promises baptism with the Spirit and fire. Jesus speaks of the fire of Gehenna (Mark 9:43-48). Revelation's lake of fire is the final judgement.
caution: Whether the fire of final judgement is literal, a picture of destruction, or a picture of purifying is a core part of /debates/hell. The texts use fire for all three ideas in different places.

name: Light
plain: Light lets people see, live and find their way. The Bible's first creative word is 'Let there be light', and light runs through Scripture as a picture of God himself, of truth, of goodness and of salvation.

meanings.note: God is light and in him is no darkness at all.
God's word gives light; people in darkness see a great light.

meanings.meaning: Jesus as the light of the world
meanings.note: John presents Jesus as the true light coming into the world.
Israel and then the church are called to be a light to the nations.
In the end God himself is the light; no sun is needed.

otUsage: Creation light, the pillar of fire, the priestly blessing ('make his face shine', Num 6:25), and Isaiah's promises of light dawning on the nations.
ntUsage: John's Gospel makes light versus darkness a central theme. Paul calls believers 'children of light' (Eph 5:8; 1 Thess 5:5). Jesus' face shines like the sun at the transfiguration.

name: Darkness
plain: Darkness is where you cannot see and danger hides. In the Bible it can mean chaos, judgement, ignorance, evil and death. Yet God is not afraid of darkness, and sometimes hides himself in it.

meanings.note: God separates light from darkness and names both.
The ninth plague, the day of the LORD as darkness, darkness at the crucifixion, and the 'outer darkness'.
People love darkness because their deeds are evil; God rescues from the domain of darkness.

meanings.meaning: The hiddenness and mystery of God
meanings.note: Moses approached the thick darkness where God was. God is beyond human sight.

meanings.meaning: Darkness is not dark to God
meanings.note: No darkness hides anyone from God, and he rules over it.

otUsage: Creation, the Egyptian plague, Sinai's thick darkness, and the prophets' day of the LORD.
ntUsage: Darkness covers the land at Jesus' death; John's Gospel contrasts light and darkness; Paul describes conversion as moving from darkness to light (Acts 26:18).
caution: Darkness in Scripture is never about skin colour. Using 'dark' and 'light' imagery to rank peoples is a misuse of these texts that has caused real harm. Christian mystics (for example the tradition behind *The Cloud of Unknowing*) also use darkness positively for God's mystery.

name: Cloud
plain: Clouds both reveal and hide. In the Bible a cloud often shows that God is present while veiling his full glory. It guided Israel in the desert, filled the temple, and appears when Jesus is transfigured and ascends.

meanings.note: Israel moved when the cloud moved and stopped when it stopped.
The cloud filled the tabernacle and temple so that priests could not stand to minister.

meanings.meaning: The Father's voice at the transfiguration
meanings.note: A bright cloud overshadows the disciples and the Father speaks.

meanings.meaning: The Son of Man coming with clouds
meanings.note: In Daniel the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. Some read Jesus' use of this as his vindication and enthronement (fulfilled at the resurrection, ascension and the fall of Jerusalem); others read it of his visible return. Many hold both.
The faithful of Hebrews 11 surround believers like a cloud.

otUsage: The pillar of cloud, Sinai's cloud, the temple cloud, and clouds as God's chariot (Ps 104:3). Paul says Israel was 'baptised in the cloud and in the sea' (1 Cor 10:2).
ntUsage: Transfiguration, ascension and return all involve clouds, linking Jesus to the Old Testament glory-cloud.
caution: The later Jewish term Shekinah (God's 'dwelling' presence) is often used for the glory-cloud, but the word itself does not appear in the Bible; it comes from rabbinic writings.

name: Wind / breath / Spirit
original: Hebrew ruach, neshamah; Greek pneuma, pnoe
plain: In both Hebrew and Greek the same word can mean wind, breath or spirit. So the invisible moving air becomes a picture of God's life-giving Spirit: unseen, powerful, and the source of life.

meanings.meaning: The breath of life from God
meanings.note: God breathes life into Adam; when he takes away breath, creatures die.
In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones the breath, wind and Spirit are one word. Jesus breathes on the disciples; Pentecost comes as a rushing wind.
God parts the sea with wind and sends wind to bring quail; Jesus rebukes the wind.
Human life is a breath; much effort is 'chasing the wind'.
The four winds mean all directions.

otUsage: Ruach appears hundreds of times for wind, human spirit and God's Spirit. The Spirit comes on judges, kings and prophets for specific tasks.
ntUsage: Pneuma is the regular word for the Holy Spirit. Jesus plays on the double meaning when he tells Nicodemus the wind blows where it wishes.
caution: In Genesis 1:2 ruach elohim can be translated 'Spirit of God', 'wind from God' or even 'mighty wind'; translations differ, and readers should not build too much on one rendering.

name: Rain and dew
original: Hebrew matar, geshem (rain), tal (dew); Greek huetos, brecho
plain: Israel depended on rain, not on a great river like Egypt's Nile. Timely rain and morning dew meant crops and life; drought meant famine. So rain and dew became pictures of God's blessing, his word and his Spirit.

meanings.note: Faithfulness brings rain in season; Elijah's drought confronts Baal, the supposed storm god.
God's word falls like rain and does not return without effect.
Joel moves from the early and latter rain to the Spirit poured on all people.
God sends rain on the just and unjust; this is often called common grace.
Gideon's fleece and the dew of Hermon.

otUsage: The early (autumn) and latter (spring) rains framed the farming year. Rain at the wrong time could be a sign of judgement (1 Sam 12:17-18), and the flood is rain as destruction.
ntUsage: James uses Elijah's prayer for rain as an example of effective prayer (Jas 5:17-18) and the farmer waiting for rains as a picture of patience (Jas 5:7).
caution: The 'Latter Rain' movement (1940s onward) took Joel 2:23 as a prophecy of an end-time revival with restored apostles and prophets; most interpreters read Joel's rains first as literal harvest rains that picture the Spirit's coming at Pentecost. See /movements/prophetic-movement.

name: Sea
plain: Israel was not a seafaring nation, and the sea seemed restless, dangerous and untamed. In the Bible it often stands for chaos and hostile powers that only God can master. In the new creation 'there is no more sea'.

meanings.note: God sets limits to the sea and crushes the sea monster Leviathan or Rahab.
God parts the Red Sea; Jesus calms the storm and walks on the water, doing what the Old Testament says God does.

meanings.meaning: Restless nations and the source of evil empires
meanings.note: Beasts representing empires rise from the sea.

meanings.meaning: Chaos removed in the new creation
meanings.note: 'No more sea' probably means no more chaos, danger or separation, not literally no oceans; readers differ.

otUsage: Creation, the Red Sea crossing, Jonah's storm, and the great bronze 'sea' basin in Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 7:23-26).
ntUsage: Jesus' stilling of the storm and walking on water; Revelation's sea of glass before God's throne (Rev 4:6; Rev 15:2) shows chaos made calm.
caution: Neighbouring cultures told myths of gods fighting the sea (Baal against Yam in Ugaritic texts; Marduk against Tiamat in Babylon). Scholars broadly agree the Bible uses similar imagery while insisting there is one God and the sea is his creature, not a rival god; how much was borrowed is debated.

name: River
plain: Rivers bring water to dry land and make life possible. The Bible begins with a river flowing out of Eden and ends with the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne.

meanings.note: Ezekiel's river flows from the temple and makes the Dead Sea fresh; Revelation's river flows from the throne.
Rivers of living water flow from the believer's heart, which John explains as the Spirit.
'Let justice roll down like waters.'
The Euphrates marked the edge of the promised land and, in Revelation, a frontier from which judgement comes.

otUsage: The Nile (Egypt's life source, turned to blood in the first plague), the Euphrates, the Jordan, and the rivers of Babylon where the exiles wept (Ps 137:1).
ntUsage: Baptism in the Jordan, Lydia's conversion by a riverside place of prayer (Acts 16:13), and the river of life.

name: Rock
plain: A rock is solid, unmoving and a safe high place to hide. 'Rock' is one of the Bible's favourite names for God: dependable, a refuge, a foundation.

meanings.meaning: God as rock: faithful and dependable
meanings.note: Moses' song repeatedly names God 'the Rock'.
Paul says 'the rock was Christ', reading the wilderness event as pointing to Christ.
Hearing and doing Jesus' words is building on rock.

meanings.meaning: 'On this rock I will build my church'
meanings.note: The rock is Peter himself (Catholic view, and many Protestant scholars today); Peter's confession of faith (common among Reformers and some Fathers); or Christ himself (also an ancient reading). Debated.
The same rock that saves trips up those who refuse it.

otUsage: God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock as his glory passes (Exod 33:21-22). David hides in rocky strongholds and names God his rock.
ntUsage: Peter's name (Greek Petros, Aramaic Kephas) means 'rock'. Jesus' tomb was cut in rock (Mark 15:46).

name: Mountain
plain: Mountains are high, hard to reach and close to the sky, so in the Bible they are where heaven and earth meet. God gives the law on a mountain, the temple stands on a mountain, and Jesus teaches, is transfigured and commissions his disciples on mountains.

meanings.note: Moriah, Horeb/Sinai and Elijah's encounter on Horeb.

meanings.meaning: Zion: God's dwelling and centre for the nations
meanings.note: In the last days the LORD's mountain is raised above all others and the nations stream to it.
Babylon is a 'destroying mountain'; God's kingdom becomes a mountain filling the earth.
Matthew places key moments on mountains, echoing Moses at Sinai.
A mountain becomes a plain before Zerubbabel; faith can move mountains.

otUsage: Ararat, Moriah, Sinai, Carmel, Zion. 'High places' on hills were also sites of idolatry that faithful kings tore down (2 Kgs 18:4).
ntUsage: The Sermon on the Mount, the transfiguration, the Mount of Olives, and the great commission. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worship is not tied to either mountain (John 4:20-24).
caution: The 'seven mountains' teaching (that Christians must take over seven spheres of culture) uses Isaiah 2:2 and Revelation 17:9 in ways most commentators consider foreign to their context. See /movements/dominion-theology.

name: Wilderness / desert
plain: The wilderness is dry, empty land where people cannot survive on their own. In the Bible it is a place of testing and failure, but also of God's care and fresh beginnings, where he speaks to his people with nothing else to distract them.

meanings.note: Israel was tested forty years; Jesus is tested forty days and succeeds where Israel failed.
God feeds Israel with manna and Elijah with bread; Hosea pictures God wooing Israel in the desert like a bride.
A generation died in the desert because of unbelief, a warning to later readers.

meanings.meaning: The way of a new exodus
meanings.note: The prophets foresee a highway through the desert for God's return; John the Baptist preaches there.
The scapegoat carries Israel's sins into the wilderness.

otUsage: Hagar, Moses, Israel's wanderings, David hiding from Saul, and Elijah fleeing Jezebel all meet God in the wilderness.
ntUsage: John the Baptist's ministry, Jesus' temptation, and his habit of withdrawing to deserted places to pray (Luke 5:16). The woman of Revelation 12 is protected in the wilderness.

name: Garden
original: Hebrew gan; Greek kepos, paradeisos (from a Persian word for an enclosed park)
plain: In a dry land a well-watered garden is a picture of delight, rest and plenty. The Bible begins in a garden, Jesus is arrested in a garden and buried in one, and the end of the story is a garden-city.

meanings.note: God walks in the garden with the first humans.

Some scholars (for example Gordon Wenham and G. K. Beale) note temple-like features: entrance from the east, cherubim guards, and the verbs 'serve and keep' also used of priests. Others think the parallels are overdrawn.
God will make the wilderness like Eden and his people like a watered garden.
The beloved is a locked garden; often read also of God and his people.
The tree of life returns in the city of God.

otUsage: Eden, the king's garden, vineyards and the garden imagery of the prophets and the Song of Songs.
ntUsage: Gethsemane (a garden, John 18:1); the tomb in a garden (John 19:41), where Mary mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener (John 20:15), which many read as a deliberate new-creation echo.

name: Stars, sun and moon
original: Hebrew kokhavim, shemesh, yareach; Greek asteres, helios, selene
plain: Many ancient peoples worshipped the sun, moon and stars as gods. Genesis calls them simply 'lights' made by God to mark time. In the Bible they also picture countless descendants, rulers and powers, and the shaking of the world when God judges.

meanings.note: Genesis avoids even naming the sun and moon, perhaps to deny them divine status; worshipping them is forbidden.
Abraham's offspring will be as many as the stars.
Joseph's family appear as sun, moon and stars; a 'star out of Jacob' is a coming king; the seven stars are the angels of the churches.

Sun darkened, moon turned to blood, stars falling. Isaiah uses this for Babylon's fall, which suggests it can be vivid language for the collapse of a political order; others expect literal cosmic events at the end. Debated.
Christ is the bright morning star; the righteous will shine like stars.

otUsage: Creation, the promise to Abraham, Balaam's star oracle, the sun standing still for Joshua (Josh 10:12-13), and warnings against worshipping the 'host of heaven'.
ntUsage: The Magi follow a star (Matt 2:2; Matt 2:9-10); the sun darkens at the crucifixion; Revelation's woman is clothed with the sun.
caution: The Bible forbids astrology as a way of reading the future (Isa 47:13-14). What the star of Bethlehem was (a miracle, a planetary conjunction, a comet or nova) is speculative.

name: Egypt
plain: Egypt was the great power to Israel's south-west. In the Bible it is first a place of refuge and food, then the 'house of slavery' from which God rescued Israel. It becomes a picture of bondage, and of trusting in human power instead of God.

meanings.note: God introduces himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt.
Abraham, Jacob's family and the infant Jesus all find refuge there.

meanings.meaning: God's son called out of Egypt
meanings.note: Hosea is about Israel's exodus; Matthew sees Jesus relive Israel's story.
Kings who ran to Egypt for military help are rebuked; Egypt is a broken reed.

meanings.meaning: A spiritual condition and a future hope
meanings.note: Revelation calls the city that killed the Lord 'spiritually Sodom and Egypt'; Isaiah astonishingly calls Egypt 'my people'.

otUsage: From Abraham's visit to Joseph's rise, the exodus, Solomon's marriage alliance and the prophets' warnings, Egypt is a constant presence.
ntUsage: The holy family's flight, Stephen's retelling of the exodus (Acts 7), and Hebrews' picture of Moses choosing Christ's reproach over the treasures of Egypt (Heb 11:26).
caution: Later Christian writers used 'Egypt' for the sinful world or for slavery to sin, which is a fair extension of the exodus pattern but not a fixed code; in Isaiah 19 Egypt also receives a promise.

name: Babylon
plain: Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. Through the Bible it becomes a picture of proud human power that sets itself against God and oppresses his people.

meanings.note: Babel's tower and Nebuchadnezzar's boast are humbled.

meanings.meaning: Exile and God's instrument of judgement
meanings.note: Babylon disciplines Judah, yet is itself judged after seventy years.

meanings.meaning: Seeking the welfare of a foreign city
meanings.note: Exiles are told to pray for Babylon's peace.

meanings.meaning: The oppressive world power of the end
meanings.note: Babylon the great is a seductive, wealthy, violent city that falls in one hour.
Most scholars think Peter writes from Rome and Revelation's city on seven hills is Rome. Others suggest Jerusalem, a future city, or the world system in every age.

otUsage: Babel in Genesis, the exile in Kings and Chronicles, and oracles against Babylon in Isaiah and Jeremiah.
ntUsage: Mentioned in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:11-12), as a code word in 1 Peter, and as the great city of Revelation 17 to 18.
caution: Many Reformers identified Revelation's Babylon with the papacy; this was a polemical reading of their time and is not held by most Protestant scholars today. Identifications with modern cities or nations are speculative.

name: Jerusalem / Zion
original: Hebrew Yerushalayim, Tsiyyon; Greek Ierousalem, Sion
plain: Jerusalem was David's capital and the site of the temple. Zion was first the hill of David's fortress, then a name for the whole city and its people. In the Bible it stands for the place God chose to live among his people, and finally for the new city where God and humanity dwell together.

meanings.note: God chose Zion as his resting place.
God installs his king on Zion.
Nations come to learn God's ways.
Being God's city did not protect it from judgement; Jesus weeps over it.
Believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem; the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven.

otUsage: From Melchizedek's Salem (Gen 14:18) through David, Solomon's temple, its destruction and rebuilding, and the Songs of Zion in the Psalms.
ntUsage: Jesus is presented there, teaches there, dies outside its walls and rises nearby; the church begins there (Acts 2). Paul contrasts the present Jerusalem and the Jerusalem above.
caution: How these promises relate to the modern city and state of Israel is a live debate among Christians; see /debates/israel-and-church.

name: Sodom (and Gomorrah)
plain: Sodom was a city near the Dead Sea that God destroyed with fire in Abraham's day. Ever after it is the Bible's standard example of a society ripe for judgement, and a warning to others, including God's own people.

meanings.note: Its overthrow is the benchmark for devastation.
The prophets shock Judah by calling them Sodom; Ezekiel says Jerusalem was worse.

Genesis describes an attempted gang rape of guests; Ezekiel names pride, plenty, ease and neglect of the poor, plus 'abomination'; Jude speaks of sexual immorality and 'strange flesh'. Some read the core sin as violent inhospitality; others as sexual sin including same-sex acts; many see both. Debated.
Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom than for towns that reject him.

otUsage: Lot settles near Sodom; Abraham intercedes for it (Gen 18:22-33); it becomes a byword in the Law and Prophets.
ntUsage: Jesus, Peter, Jude and Revelation all use Sodom as a warning.
caution: Discussions about sexuality often turn on Sodom; give weight to all the texts together, and note that both sides of the modern debate agree the attempted gang rape was evil.

name: Eden
original: Hebrew Eden (probably 'delight'; also linked to a word for a fertile plain)
plain: Eden is the garden home where God placed the first humans. It stands for life as God meant it: plenty, beauty, work with purpose and open friendship with God. Losing Eden pictures what sin lost; its return pictures salvation.

meanings.note: Trees good for food, rivers, work, and God present.
Humans are sent out and cherubim guard the way to the tree of life.
God will make desolate land like Eden.

meanings.meaning: Garden of God and holy mountain
meanings.note: Ezekiel places Eden on 'the holy mountain of God'.

meanings.meaning: Fulfilled and surpassed in the new creation
meanings.note: The tree of life and the river return, and the curse is gone.

otUsage: Genesis 2 to 3, the prophets' images of restored land, and Ezekiel's laments over Tyre and Egypt.
ntUsage: Not named in the New Testament, but echoed in 'paradise' (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor 12:4) and in Revelation 22.
caution: Eden's location is unknown; Genesis names the Tigris and Euphrates alongside two unidentified rivers. How literally to read Genesis 2 to 3 is part of /debates/creation.

name: Jordan River
plain: The Jordan runs down from the north to the Dead Sea and marked the eastern border of the promised land. Crossing it meant entering the promise. Later it is where John baptised and where Jesus was baptised.

meanings.note: God stops the river so Israel crosses on dry ground, echoing the Red Sea.
Elijah parts the Jordan, is taken up, and Elisha parts it again with his cloak.
Naaman is healed after reluctantly washing seven times in a small, muddy river.
John baptises at the Jordan, the border of the land, suggesting a new entry into God's promise.
Christian hymns and spirituals use crossing Jordan for dying and entering heaven. This is a later devotional image, not a biblical use.

otUsage: Lot chooses the Jordan plain (Gen 13:10-11); Israel crosses at Gilgal; Elijah and Elisha minister around it; Jeremiah speaks of 'the thicket of the Jordan' (Jer 12:5).
ntUsage: John's baptism, Jesus' baptism and the Spirit descending like a dove, and Jesus' ministry 'beyond the Jordan' (John 10:40).

name: Sinai / Horeb
plain: Sinai (also called Horeb) is the mountain where God met Moses in the burning bush and later gave Israel the covenant and the law. It stands for God's holy, awe-inspiring presence and for the old covenant.

meanings.note: Israel becomes God's treasured people and kingdom of priests.
Fire, smoke, thunder and fear kept the people at a distance.
Elijah meets God at Horeb not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a low whisper.
Paul links Sinai with slavery and Hagar; Hebrews contrasts Sinai's fear with Zion's welcome. Neither denies Sinai's goodness, but both say something greater has come.

otUsage: The burning bush, the giving of the law, the golden calf, the tabernacle instructions and Elijah's flight. Poetry remembers God 'coming from Sinai' (Deut 33:2; Ps 68:8).
ntUsage: Stephen recalls the angel at Sinai (Acts 7:30-38); Paul and Hebrews use Sinai to explain the old and new covenants.
caution: The mountain's location is debated: the traditional Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai peninsula, other Sinai sites, or a site in north-west Arabia (Paul's 'Mount Sinai in Arabia', Gal 4:25, may mean the Nabataean region, which included Sinai).

name: The nations / Gentiles
plain: 'The nations' (or Gentiles) means all the peoples who were not Israel. They often appear as idol-worshippers and enemies, yet from Abraham onward God promises to bless all nations, and the New Testament describes Gentiles welcomed into God's people as equals.

meanings.note: The table of nations traces all peoples to Noah's sons.
Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance.
Israel was not to copy the nations' practices.
Israel's servant is a light to the nations; foreigners will pray in God's house.
Jews and Gentiles become one new people without Gentiles having to become Jews.
The final picture keeps nations distinct but united in worship.

otUsage: Foreigners such as Rahab, Ruth, Naaman and the Ninevites respond to God, while the nations at large are judged for cruelty and idolatry (Amos 1 to 2).
ntUsage: Jesus' ministry touches Gentiles (Matt 8:10-11); Pentecost gathers people 'from every nation' (Acts 2:5-11), which many see as a reversal of Babel; Paul is the apostle to the Gentiles.
caution: Deuteronomy 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in the standard Hebrew text but 'sons of God' in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek. Some scholars (for example Michael Heiser) build a view of nations assigned to lesser spiritual powers on this; others are more cautious. Debated.

name: Hand / right hand
original: Hebrew yad, yamin (right hand); Greek cheir, dexios
plain: The hand is how people act, work, hold, give and fight. In the Bible 'the hand of God' means God's power at work, and the right hand, usually the stronger one, means strength, favour and the place of honour.

meanings.note: God brought Israel out 'with a strong hand'; his hand is not too short to save.
No one can snatch Christ's sheep out of the Father's hand; God has engraved his people on his palms.
Jacob crosses his hands to give the right-hand blessing to the younger son; the sheep stand at the King's right.
'Clean hands' means innocent actions.
Raising the hand accompanied a solemn oath.

otUsage: 'The hand of the LORD came upon' a prophet describes inspiration (Ezek 1:3; 2 Kgs 3:15). Stretching out the hand begins plagues in Egypt.
ntUsage: Jesus heals by touch, takes children in his hands, shows his wounded hands after rising (John 20:27), and sits at the Father's right hand.
caution: God's 'hand' and 'arm' are figures of speech for his action; the Bible also says God is spirit (John 4:24).

name: Eye
plain: Eyes see, notice and desire. God's eyes stand for his watchful care and complete knowledge; human eyes stand for understanding, for desire and for generosity or greed.

meanings.note: Nothing is hidden from God's sight; his eyes are on those who fear him.
'Open my eyes' is a prayer for understanding.
Sin often begins with seeing and wanting.

meanings.meaning: Good eye and evil eye: generosity and stinginess
meanings.note: In Hebrew idiom a 'good eye' is generous and an 'evil eye' is grudging. Many scholars read Jesus' 'healthy eye' saying in this light, since it sits between sayings on money; others take it more generally of focused devotion.
God's people are 'the apple of his eye', the pupil a person instinctively protects.

otUsage: God sees Hagar ('the God who sees', Gen 16:13); doing 'what was right in his own eyes' describes moral chaos (Judg 21:25).
ntUsage: Jesus heals the blind as a sign of spiritual sight; the Lamb has seven eyes, the seven spirits sent into all the earth (Rev 5:6).

name: Heart
plain: In the Bible the heart is not mainly about feelings. It is the centre of the whole person: thinking, choosing, desiring and loving. What is in the heart shapes everything a person does, which is why God looks at the heart and promises to give a new one.

meanings.meaning: The control centre of the person
meanings.note: Evil and good flow out of the heart; God looks on the heart, not outward appearance.

meanings.meaning: Corrupted and in need of renewal
meanings.note: God promises to write his law on hearts and replace a heart of stone.
Love God with all your heart.
True belonging to God is inward, a heart opened to him.
Pharaoh hardens his heart and God hardens it; how these relate is debated (see /debates/soteriology).
God's love and Spirit are poured into the heart; Christ dwells there by faith.

otUsage: Lev and levav occur hundreds of times. For deep emotions Hebrew often uses other organs, such as the kidneys (translated 'mind' or 'reins', Ps 7:9; Jer 17:10) and the bowels (Isa 63:15).
ntUsage: Jesus locates purity and sin in the heart (Matt 5:8; Matt 15:19). Paul says belief happens with the heart (Rom 10:9-10).
caution: Modern 'follow your heart' advice means trusting one's feelings; the Bible both honours the heart and warns that it can deceive (Jer 17:9). Do not read the modern meaning back into biblical texts.

name: Head
plain: The head is the top and front of the body. In the Bible it can mean leader or chief, the beginning or source, and the place where honour, blessing or shame are shown.

meanings.note: Israel will be 'the head and not the tail'; Jephthah is made head over Gilead.

meanings.meaning: Christ as head of the church and of all things
meanings.note: The body grows from and under its head.
Whether kephale here means 'authority over' or 'source/origin' (or both) is a key point in /debates/gender-roles, with careful scholars on each side.

meanings.meaning: Blessing and honour on the head
meanings.note: Blessings and anointing oil rest on the head.
Dust on the head and covered heads show grief; 'his blood be on his own head' means he bears responsibility.

otUsage: The 'head of the corner' (Ps 118:22), heads of families and tribes, and the shaved or covered head in mourning.
ntUsage: Christ's headship over the church, the head-covering discussion of 1 Corinthians 11, and Jesus having 'nowhere to lay his head' (Matt 8:20).
caution: Whether the head coverings of 1 Corinthians 11:4-16 are a timeless rule or a cultural application of a principle is debated.

name: Feet
plain: Feet carry people along their way, get dirty, and are the lowest part of the body. In the Bible they picture how one lives, humble service, submission, and victory over enemies placed 'under the feet'.

meanings.note: Enemies are made a footstool; Satan will be crushed under believers' feet.
Washing feet was slaves' work; Jesus does it for his disciples.

meanings.meaning: The posture of a disciple or worshipper
meanings.note: Sitting at someone's feet means learning from them; falling at their feet means worship or surrender.
The feet of those who bring good news are beautiful.
Removing sandals before God's presence.

otUsage: Hospitality began with washing guests' feet; enemies were trodden underfoot; Ruth lay at Boaz's feet (Ruth 3:7-8).
ntUsage: Mary sits at Jesus' feet; a sinful woman anoints them; Jesus washes the disciples' feet; the risen Christ's feet are like burnished bronze (Rev 1:15).
caution: Hebrew sometimes uses 'feet' as a polite euphemism for private parts (probably Isa 7:20). Whether Ruth 3 or Exodus 4:25 has this sense is debated; avoid building conclusions on it.

name: Blood
plain: Blood is life: when it is poured out, a creature dies. So in the Bible blood means life given up in death. It cries out when murder is done, and it makes atonement when offered in sacrifice. The New Testament centres on the blood of Jesus.

meanings.note: Blood was not to be eaten because the life is in it.
God gave blood on the altar to make atonement. How Christ's blood atones is explained differently by the various atonement views (see /debates/atonement).
Passover blood marked the houses; Moses sprinkled 'the blood of the covenant'; Jesus speaks of his blood of the new covenant.
Christ's blood buys people for God from every nation and washes robes white.
Abel's blood cries out for justice; Jesus' blood 'speaks a better word'.
Water turned to blood; the moon turned to blood.

otUsage: Sacrifices, the Passover, covenant-making, food laws and laws on murder all centre on blood.
ntUsage: The Lord's Supper cup, Jesus' death, the Jerusalem council's ban on eating blood for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20), and Revelation's praise of the Lamb's blood.
caution: Matthew 27:25 ('his blood be on us and on our children') was misused for centuries to blame Jews collectively for Jesus' death; Christian churches, including the Catholic Church at Vatican II (*Nostra Aetate* 4), have rejected that reading. 'Pleading the blood' as a spoken formula is a later devotional practice, not a biblical one.

name: Face
plain: Seeing someone's face means being in their presence and knowing them personally. In Hebrew the word for 'face' also means 'presence'. God's shining face means his favour; his hidden face means distance and trouble. The hope of the Bible is to see God face to face.

meanings.note: 'My presence (literally, my face) will go with you.'
'Make your face shine on us, and we shall be saved.'
The LORD spoke to Moses 'face to face', yet Moses could not see God's face and live. 'Face to face' is an idiom of direct, personal relationship.
Moses' face shone; believers are transformed as they behold the Lord's glory in the face of Christ.
'They will see his face.'

otUsage: The 'bread of the Presence' is literally 'bread of the face'. Jacob names a place Peniel ('face of God', Gen 32:30). Psalms of lament ask why God hides his face.
ntUsage: Jesus 'set his face' to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51); his face shines at the transfiguration; angels always see the Father's face (Matt 18:10).

name: Arm of the LORD
plain: A bared, outstretched arm is a picture of strength put to work. 'The arm of the LORD' means God personally stepping in with power to rescue his people, as he did in the exodus.

meanings.note: 'With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.'
God bares his holy arm before all nations; when no one else could save, his own arm brought salvation.

Isaiah asks 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' just before describing the suffering servant; John applies this to Jesus. Many read the servant himself as the arm revealed; others read the arm as God's power shown through him.
The same arm that rules gathers lambs; 'underneath are the everlasting arms'.

meanings.meaning: Not trusting in an 'arm of flesh'
meanings.note: Human strength is contrasted with God's.

otUsage: Mostly in the exodus traditions, the Psalms and Isaiah 40 to 66.
ntUsage: Mary sings that God 'has shown strength with his arm' (Luke 1:51); Paul says God led Israel out of Egypt 'with an uplifted arm' (Acts 13:17).
caution: Like 'hand' and 'face', this is a figure of speech for God's action, not a claim that God has a physical body.

name: Gold
plain: Gold is the most precious and lasting metal, and it does not tarnish. In the Bible it marks God's glory and dwelling, royal wealth, faith refined by testing, and also the greed and idolatry that wealth can lead to.

meanings.note: The ark, mercy seat, lampstand and inner temple were gold; the new Jerusalem is pure gold like glass.
Nations bring gold to the king; the Magi bring gold to Jesus. Early tradition read gold as honouring him as king (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.9.2).
Trials burn away impurities.
The golden calf; Achan's stolen gold; idols of silver and gold.

meanings.meaning: Wisdom and God's word worth more than gold
meanings.note: The truly valuable things outweigh gold.

otUsage: Tabernacle and temple furnishings, Solomon's wealth, Nebuchadnezzar's head of gold (Dan 2:38) and his golden statue.
ntUsage: The Magi's gift, warnings about wealth, refined faith, golden lampstands and bowls in Revelation, and the golden city.
caution: Typological systems that make gold always mean 'divinity' go beyond the text; context decides.

name: Silver
plain: Silver was the everyday money of the ancient world, weighed out in shekels. So in the Bible it often means price and payment, including the price of redemption, and it is used as a picture of refining and purity.

meanings.note: Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver; Jesus is betrayed for thirty.
Israelites paid silver as a ransom for their lives; Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with Christ's blood.
God's words are like silver refined seven times.
Jerusalem's silver has become dross.

meanings.meaning: Tabernacle bases cast from ransom silver
meanings.note: The silver from the census ransom was cast into the sockets that held up the tabernacle. Seeing this as 'the house of God resting on redemption' is a later typological reading.

otUsage: Trade, temple furnishings, ransom payments, and the second-ranked kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Dan 2:32).
ntUsage: Judas' thirty pieces, Peter's 'silver and gold I do not have' (Acts 3:6), and the silversmiths of Ephesus (Acts 19:24).
caution: Saying 'silver always means redemption' is a later typological habit; most uses are simply about money.

name: Bronze
original: Hebrew nechoshet (copper or bronze; KJV 'brass'); Greek chalkos, chalkolibanon
plain: Bronze (an alloy of copper and tin) was strong and used for tools, weapons and the outer furnishings of the tabernacle. It is associated with strength, endurance, and the places where sin was dealt with: the altar and the bronze serpent.

meanings.meaning: The place of sacrifice and cleansing
meanings.note: The altar of burnt offering and the washing basin in the courtyard were bronze. Reading bronze as a code for 'judgement' is a later typological convention.

meanings.meaning: The bronze serpent: healing by looking
meanings.note: Bitten Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived; Jesus compares his being 'lifted up'.

meanings.meaning: A good sign turned into an idol
meanings.note: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) because people were burning incense to it.
God makes Jeremiah 'bronze walls'.
The risen Christ's feet are like burnished bronze refined in a furnace.

otUsage: Tabernacle courtyard, Solomon's great bronze pillars and sea (1 Kgs 7:13-47), Goliath's armour, and the drought curse of skies like bronze (Deut 28:23).
ntUsage: Jesus' reference to the bronze serpent and Revelation's description of his feet.
caution: KJV 'brass' (copper and zinc) is a mistranslation by modern standards; the ancient metal was copper or bronze.

name: Iron
plain: Iron was the hard, new metal of the Iron Age and gave military advantage. In the Bible it pictures crushing strength, unbreakable rule, harsh oppression and stubbornness.

meanings.note: The fourth kingdom is iron that breaks everything, yet mixed with clay. Most identify it with Rome (traditional) or with the Greek kingdoms (many modern scholars).
The Messiah rules with a rod of iron.
Egypt was an 'iron furnace'; a yoke of iron is crushing slavery.
Canaanite iron chariots and the Philistine monopoly on smithing.
A neck like an iron sinew; 'iron sharpens iron'.

otUsage: Og's iron bed (Deut 3:11), tools that were not to touch the altar stones (Deut 27:5), and Elisha's floating axe head (2 Kgs 6:5-7).
ntUsage: Mostly Revelation's rod of iron and the iron gate that opens for Peter (Acts 12:10).

name: Precious stones
original: Hebrew even yeqarah; Greek lithos timios
plain: Gems are rare, beautiful and lasting. In the Bible they adorn the high priest's breastpiece, describe God's dazzling throne, and form the foundations of the new Jerusalem, a picture of God's people as precious and of a city of unimaginable glory.

meanings.note: Twelve stones engraved with the tribes' names sat over the high priest's heart.

meanings.meaning: The dazzling glory of God's throne
meanings.note: Sapphire pavement, a throne like sapphire, jasper and carnelian, an emerald rainbow.

meanings.meaning: The beauty of the new Jerusalem
meanings.note: Foundations adorned with twelve kinds of jewels. The list echoes the high priest's breastpiece, suggesting the whole city is priestly and holy.
Onyx in Eden's land; the king of Tyre in Eden covered with stones.
Gold, silver and precious stones survive the testing fire; wood, hay and straw do not.

otUsage: The breastpiece, Solomon's temple and the wealth of kings.
ntUsage: Mostly Revelation: the throne, Babylon's jewellery (Rev 17:4) and the city's foundations.
caution: The ancient names of gems cannot always be matched to modern stones, so translations vary. Ancient writers such as Josephus and Philo linked the twelve stones with months or signs of the zodiac; assigning each stone a fixed spiritual meaning or tribe in Revelation is speculative.

name: Pearl
original: Greek margarites; Hebrew peninim (Job 28:18; Prov 3:15) is uncertain, perhaps coral, rubies or pearls
plain: Pearls were among the most costly luxuries in the Roman world. Jesus uses a pearl for the surpassing worth of God's kingdom, and Revelation makes each gate of the new Jerusalem a single pearl.

meanings.meaning: The surpassing worth of the kingdom
meanings.note: A merchant sells everything to buy one pearl. Most read the merchant as a disciple giving all for the kingdom; others read the merchant as Christ giving all to gain his people. Debated.

meanings.meaning: Holy things not to be thrown away
meanings.note: Do not throw pearls before pigs: use discernment about sharing sacred things with those who will trample them.
Contrasted with good deeds; part of Babylon's wealth.
Each gate is one huge pearl: lavish welcome into the city.

otUsage: No certain mention. Wisdom is 'more precious than peninim' (Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; Prov 8:11), a word variously translated rubies, corals or pearls.
ntUsage: Jesus' parables and sayings, Paul's advice on modesty, and Revelation.
caution: The popular idea that the pearl gates symbolise suffering (because a pearl forms around an irritation in an oyster) is a modern devotional reflection, not something the text says.

name: White robes
original: Greek stole leuke, himatia leuka; Hebrew lavan (white)
plain: Clean white clothing was costly to keep and was worn for celebrations. In the Bible white garments picture purity and forgiveness, victory and joy, and the glory of heaven.

meanings.note: Sins like scarlet become white as snow; robes washed white in the Lamb's blood.

meanings.meaning: Victory and vindication of the faithful
meanings.note: Martyrs and those who overcome are clothed in white.
The Ancient of Days, the transfigured Jesus and angels wear dazzling white.
The bride's fine linen is 'the righteous deeds of the saints'. Some stress these deeds as the fruit of grace; others link the linen to Christ's righteousness given to believers. Debated.
'Let your garments always be white.'

otUsage: White is the colour of snow and wool for cleansing, and of the Ancient of Days in Daniel. Priests wore white linen (Lev 16:4).
ntUsage: Transfiguration, resurrection angels and Revelation's redeemed crowd.
caution: In the early church the newly baptised were often dressed in white garments, a practice described in fourth-century baptismal instruction; it is a tradition, not a biblical command.

name: Sackcloth
plain: Sackcloth was rough cloth, usually of goat hair, used for sacks. People wore it next to the skin, often with ashes on the head, to show grief, repentance or desperate prayer.

meanings.note: Jacob mourns Joseph; Mordecai mourns Haman's decree.
Even Nineveh's king and animals wear sackcloth.
Ahab humbles himself; Hezekiah prays in sackcloth.
The two witnesses prophesy clothed in sackcloth.
God removes sackcloth and clothes with gladness.

otUsage: Common in narratives of grief and in prophetic calls to repentance.
ntUsage: Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes; the sun becomes black as sackcloth (Rev 6:12).

name: Wedding garment
plain: In Jesus' parable of the wedding feast, a guest is thrown out because he is not wearing wedding clothes. The garment stands for what fits a person to share in God's kingdom celebration, though what exactly it represents is debated.

meanings.meaning: What fits a guest for the kingdom
meanings.note: The invitation is open to all, but accepting it involves being properly clothed.
Many Reformed and evangelical interpreters read the garment as Christ's righteousness received by faith ('garments of salvation', 'put on Christ').

meanings.meaning: A changed life of love and good works
meanings.note: Many Church Fathers (Augustine among them) and Catholic interpreters read it as charity or a life fitting the gospel. Many interpreters combine the two readings.
The church is clothed for the wedding of the Lamb.

otUsage: Clothing for celebration and covenant (Isa 61:10); Zephaniah warns those dressed in 'foreign attire' on the day of the LORD's sacrifice (Zeph 1:7-8).
ntUsage: Only in Matthew's parable, but connected to Paul's language of putting on Christ and Revelation's bride.
caution: Preachers often say the host provided wedding garments to all guests, so refusing one was an insult. Evidence for such a custom is thin (2 Kgs 10:22 is sometimes cited), so do not lean on it.

name: Armour of God
plain: Paul tells believers to put on 'the whole armour of God' to stand against evil. Each piece names a spiritual reality, such as truth, righteousness, faith and God's word. The image draws first on Isaiah, where God himself puts on armour, and probably also on the Roman soldier.

meanings.meaning: God's own armour shared with his people
meanings.note: In Isaiah God wears righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet; Paul gives this armour to believers.

meanings.meaning: The struggle is spiritual, not against people
meanings.note: The enemy is spiritual forces of evil, not flesh and blood.
Truth, righteousness, readiness from the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God.

meanings.meaning: Prayer as the way to stand
meanings.note: The passage ends with constant prayer in the Spirit.
Paul uses armour imagery in other letters too.

otUsage: God as divine warrior (Exod 15:3; Isa 59:15-18). The Wisdom of Solomon, a book outside the Protestant canon, also describes God arming himself.
ntUsage: Ephesians 6:10-18 is the main text; parallels in Romans, 2 Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians.
caution: Whether 'righteousness' here is God's gift of right standing or the believer's upright life is debated. Elaborate modern 'spiritual warfare' methods (naming territorial spirits and so on) go beyond what this passage describes.

name: Priestly garments and ephod
original: Hebrew ephod, choshen (breastpiece), me'il (robe); Greek stole, poderes
plain: Israel's high priest wore special garments 'for glory and for beauty': a linen tunic, a blue robe with bells and pomegranates, an embroidered apron called the ephod, a breastpiece of twelve stones, and a turban with a gold plate reading 'Holy to the LORD'. They showed that he represented the people before God.

meanings.note: The gold plate bore 'Holy to the LORD', so the priest carried the people's guilt in offerings.
The tribes' names were on his shoulders and over his heart.
The Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece were used to ask God's will. How they worked is unknown.
Gideon's golden ephod became a snare; Micah made one for his private shrine.

meanings.meaning: Christ the high priest and a priestly people
meanings.note: The risen Christ wears a long robe and golden sash; believers are a royal priesthood.

otUsage: Exodus 28 and 39 describe the garments. Simpler linen ephods were worn by Samuel and by David when he danced before the ark (1 Sam 2:18; 2 Sam 6:14). Zechariah sees the high priest's filthy clothes replaced (Zech 3:3-5).
ntUsage: Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest. John notes Jesus' seamless tunic (John 19:23), which some link to the high priest's woven robe (Exod 28:32); others see no such intention.
caution: Christian vestments developed over centuries; their link to the Levitical garments is a matter of tradition and differs between churches.

name: Anointing
original: Hebrew mashach (to anoint; hence mashiach, Messiah); Greek chrio (hence christos), aleipho
plain: To anoint is to pour or rub oil on someone. It set apart kings, priests and sometimes prophets for God's service. 'Messiah' (Hebrew) and 'Christ' (Greek) both mean 'anointed one'. Anointing was also everyday care: for guests, the sick and the dead.

meanings.note: Saul, David and Solomon are anointed; the king is 'the LORD's anointed'.
Aaron is anointed; Elijah is told to anoint Elisha.
Jesus is anointed with the Spirit at his baptism and announces it in Nazareth.
All believers share an anointing that teaches them.
A woman anoints Jesus beforehand for burial.

otUsage: David refuses to harm Saul because he is 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Sam 24:6). Cyrus, a Persian, is called God's anointed (Isa 45:1).
ntUsage: The whole title 'Christ' rests on this practice. Anointing the sick continues in James 5.
caution: 'Touch not mine anointed' (Ps 105:15; 1 Chr 16:22) is about the patriarchs, and is sometimes misused to shield leaders from accountability. Anointing in later sacraments (chrismation, confirmation, anointing of the sick) is valued in Catholic and Orthodox tradition and understood differently by Protestants.

name: Laying on of hands
original: Hebrew samakh yad (to lean the hand); Greek epithesis ton cheiron
plain: Placing hands on someone or something was a way of connecting with them: identifying with a sacrifice, passing on a blessing, commissioning a leader, praying for healing, or praying for the Spirit to come.

meanings.note: The worshipper leaned a hand on the animal; Aaron confessed sins over the scapegoat.
Jacob blesses Joseph's sons; Jesus blesses children.
Joshua, the Seven, Barnabas and Saul, and Timothy were set apart this way. Warning: do not be hasty (1 Tim 5:22).
Jesus and the apostles often healed by touch.
In some Acts episodes the Spirit comes after hands are laid on; in others not (Acts 10:44). Whether this is a pattern for today is debated.

otUsage: Sacrifice, blessing and Joshua's commissioning.
ntUsage: Healing, blessing, ordination and Spirit-reception; Hebrews lists it among the church's foundational teachings (Heb 6:2).
caution: Mark 16:18 (laying hands on the sick) is in the longer ending of Mark, which many textual scholars think was added later. Whether ordination passes down an unbroken 'apostolic succession' is a Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican conviction that most other Protestants do not share.

name: Washing
original: Hebrew rachats, kabas; Greek louo, nipto, baptizo
plain: Washing removes dirt, so it naturally pictures removing sin and impurity. In the Bible washing ranges from ritual cleansing for worship, to washing hands to declare innocence, to baptism and Jesus washing his disciples' feet.

meanings.note: Priests washed before serving; impurity was removed by washing and waiting.
'Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity.'
Pilate washes his hands of Jesus' blood.
How the 'washing of regeneration' relates to water baptism is debated (see /debates/baptism).
Jesus washes his disciples' feet and tells them to do likewise.

otUsage: Priestly washings, purity laws, and Naaman's sevenfold washing in the Jordan (2 Kgs 5:10-14).
ntUsage: Jesus disputes Pharisaic hand-washing traditions (Mark 7:1-8), washes feet, and the saints wash their robes in the Lamb's blood (Rev 7:14).
caution: Some churches (for example many Anabaptist, Brethren and Adventist groups) practise foot-washing as an ordinance; Catholic and other churches do it on Maundy Thursday; most churches treat John 13 as an example of humble service rather than a rite.

name: Sitting at the right hand
original: Hebrew shev limini ('sit at my right hand', Ps 110:1); Greek kathou ek dexion mou
plain: To sit at a king's right hand is to share his rule and honour. Psalm 110:1, 'The LORD says to my Lord: sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool', is the Old Testament verse most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament, applied to Jesus after his resurrection.

meanings.note: Jesus is exalted to share God's rule over all powers.
Old covenant priests stood daily; Christ sat down, because his sacrifice was complete.
Christ at God's right hand intercedes for his people.
Believers are seated with Christ in the heavenly places.
Solomon seats his mother at his right; James and John ask for the seats beside Jesus.

otUsage: Psalm 110 and royal court practice (1 Kgs 2:19).
ntUsage: Peter's Pentecost sermon, Jesus' answer to the high priest, Paul's letters and Hebrews all use it. Stephen sees Jesus standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:55-56); whether 'standing' means rising to welcome, to testify for, or to judge is debated.
caution: 'Right hand' describes status and authority, not a physical location next to God. The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds confess it, which reflects its centrality in early Christian faith.

name: Breaking bread
original: Hebrew paras lechem (Isa 58:7); Greek klasis tou artou
plain: Jewish meals began with the host blessing God and breaking a loaf to share. Jesus did this when feeding crowds and at the Last Supper, and the risen Jesus was recognised 'in the breaking of the bread'. The first Christians 'devoted themselves to breaking bread' together.

meanings.meaning: Blessing God and sharing a meal
meanings.note: Breaking bread began an ordinary Jewish meal with thanks to God.
Jesus breaks bread as his body given; the one loaf unites the church.
The Emmaus disciples' eyes are opened as he breaks bread.
Whether every 'breaking of bread' in Acts means the Lord's Supper, a fellowship meal, or both together is debated.
True fasting means breaking your bread for the hungry.

otUsage: The phrase is rare; Isaiah uses it for sharing food with the poor, and Jeremiah for a mourning meal (Jer 16:7).
ntUsage: Feeding miracles, the Last Supper, Emmaus, and the early church's gatherings, including Paul breaking bread on board ship in a storm.
caution: How the bread relates to Christ's body is debated (see /debates/lords-supper). Paul rebukes the Corinthians because their shared meal left the poor hungry (1 Cor 11:20-22): the sign was meant to be lived out.
